title: Administrative adjudication: varied decisions and layered procedural law
shortTitle: Administrative adjudication: varied decisions and layered procedural law
summary: Administrative adjudication includes high-profile licensing and security decisions, mass benefits systems, and routine permits; no single hearing model fits every determination.
notes:
Adjudication encompasses decisions about particular people, organizations, and situations across a wide range of public programs. The introduction places prominent decisions such as security-clearance revocation and aircraft grounding beside high-volume benefits, immigration, and licensing determinations and routine permits. Public salience is an unreliable measure of the aggregate importance of these decisions.

Procedure comes from several layers: the Constitution, the APA, the organic statute, and agency regulations. The APA’s definitions make adjudication a residual category after rulemaking, but that classification does not automatically require a courtroom-style hearing. Sections 553(c) and 554(a) use separate on-the-record triggers to invoke formal procedures. Congress may supply special hearing regimes, and agencies fill many procedural gaps through regulations. Informal adjudication can involve applications, investigation, negotiation, inspection, and settlement rather than a single evidentiary event.

The editors identify a persistent institutional tension. Individual adversarial process can improve fairness and protect against error, while mass administration requires coherent and workable management. Agencies are also frontline interpreters of procedural constitutional requirements because many disputes never reach courts. The chapter therefore separates the forum’s constitutional permissibility, action classification, statutory hearing requirements, and due-process minima instead of assuming that the label adjudication answers all four.
